meta.note_ru: A short reference, not medical advice. If you suspect poisoning, call a veterinarian.

intro_ru: Each well-handled case unlocks another page. Check this guide to learn what is and is not safe for cats.

items.why_ru: Onions, garlic, chives, leeks, and shallots can damage a cat’s red blood cells and cause anemia. Garlic is more potent than onion. Raw, cooked, and dried forms, including powders and sauces, are risky.
items.signs_ru: Weakness, pale gums, rapid breathing, dark or reddish urine. Signs may take several days to appear.
items.tip_ru: Call your veterinarian even if the cat seems fine.

items.why_ru: Chocolate contains theobromine and caffeine, which cats process poorly. Darker chocolate and cocoa are more dangerous.
items.signs_ru: Vomiting, agitation, rapid or irregular heartbeat, tremors, and seizures in severe cases.
items.tip_ru: Do not offer even a little chocolate. Keep sweets out of reach.

items.why_ru: Caffeine is chemically related to the theobromine found in chocolate. It is present in coffee, tea, and energy drinks.
items.signs_ru: Signs can resemble chocolate poisoning: vomiting, agitation, a fast heartbeat, and tremors.
items.tip_ru: Never leave cups or cans where a cat can reach them.

items.why_ru: Because cats are much smaller than humans, even a small amount of alcohol can be dangerous. Alcohol is also found in some desserts and raw dough.
items.signs_ru: Lethargy, vomiting, unsteady walking, and breathing problems.
items.tip_ru: If your cat licks or drinks alcohol, call a veterinarian immediately.

items.why_ru: This sweetener is used in gum, mints, and sugar-free sweets. It is known to be dangerous to dogs; evidence about cats is more limited, but some sources still list it as a concern.
items.signs_ru: The effects in cats are less well studied, so do not wait for symptoms.
items.tip_ru: Call a veterinarian if your cat eats gum or sugar-free candy.

items.why_ru: Raw yeast dough can expand in a warm stomach and ferment, creating alcohol. This may cause bloating, vomiting, and intoxication.
items.signs_ru: A swollen abdomen, vomiting, lethargy, and unsteady walking.
items.tip_ru: Keep raw dough where your cat cannot reach it.

items.why_ru: Grapes and raisins are dangerous to dogs. Evidence in cats is limited, but the ASPCA advises avoiding them.
items.signs_ru: Vomiting and lethargy. Kidney problems are possible, although evidence in cats is limited.
items.tip_ru: Avoid the risk and do not offer them.

items.why_ru: Any part of a true lily, including its pollen and even vase water, can cause acute kidney failure. Lilies are among the most dangerous plants for cats.
items.signs_ru: Vomiting, drooling, loss of appetite, and lethargy. Kidney injury can begin within hours.
items.tip_ru: Go to a veterinary clinic immediately. If you are unsure whether bouquet flowers are lilies, treat them as potentially dangerous.

emergency.title_ru: If your cat eats something toxic
steps_ru: Do not wait for symptoms; some poisons have delayed effects.
Call a veterinarian or clinic and explain what the cat ate, how much, and when.
Do not induce vomiting unless a veterinarian tells you to.
Bring the packaging or a sample of the plant.
